newsitem.title: PERU: Mediators, rebels explore ways to end Peru siege.
newsitem.headline: Mediators, rebels explore ways to end Peru siege.

text.p: Mediators met on Thursday with the leader of Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima to explore ways of ending the 12-week-old standoff.

Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent and Red Cross official Michel Minnig, guarantors of peace talks between the two sides, met with Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa inside the besieged residence for about an hour. They had no comment on their discussions.
The guarantors commission, whose third member is Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, was also expected to meet with government negotiator Domingo Palermo.

Lack of progress in face-to-face talks between the two sides has forced the guarantors to hold separate meetings with the government and rebels to analyse "alternatives that make a solution viable," the mediators said on Wednesday after they coaxed the government and rebels back to the negotiating table. The two sides had broken off talks for a week.
There were no tangible results from the negotiations and the guarantors hinted that both sides would need to relax their positions for progress to be made.
"With there not being agreements on some matters, a stage of reflection is necessary," Cipriani said after the 10th round of negotiations on Wednesday.

Palermo, who accompanied President Alberto Fujimori on a whirlwind tour of several Lima shantytowns on Thursday, echoed the guarantors' assessment of the stage the talks had reached: "There should be reflection," he told reporters.

Three months after 20-odd heavily armed rebels stormed a lavish cocktail party at the ambassdaor's home and took hundreds of guests captive, the two sides appear no closer to resolving the main rebel demand, freedom for jailed comrades.

The government says it will not consider this but the MRTA insists it will not release the remaining 72 hostages until the demand is met. As a peaceful end to the siege appeared remote, attention has focused on the possibility that the government might resort to force to free the hostages.

Peru's leading weekly magazine, Caretas, published photographs on Thursday of special forces police practicing a possible rescue attempt around a full-scale model of the besieged ambassador's residence. The "elite commandos" have been training for two weeks at a Lima police base in drills that involved simultaneous clashes with other rebels in their rural strongholds, Caretas said.

Last week, the MRTA called off talks amid accusations that the government was building a secret tunnel to storm the ambassador's residence. Fujimori, who says he will use force to end the siege only if a hostage is harmed, has not denied the existence of a tunnel or a plan to attack the mansion.

Ironically, police found a tunnel on Wednesday through which teenaged Marxist rebels planned to escape from a youth prison. Police discovered a 120-foot (40 metre)-long tunnel extending from a youth prison in Lima's Maranga neighbourhood toward nearby buildings, the Interior Ministry said.
The MRTA, whose armed members number fewer than 200, according to analysts, mainly recruits teenagers, training rebels as young as 13 in the handling guns and explosives.

Rebels occupying the residence released most hostages in the first weeks of the siege but have held onto those they consider the best bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother Pedro, two cabinet ministers, the Japanese ambassador and many Japanese businessmen.
